passage:
In the little bike workshop in Porto, Rania slammed a spoke key on the bench. "I trued a wheel perfectly in March. Now I can't remember the order. I'm useless."
Beatriz, wiping grease from her hands, pulled a battered notebook off the shelf. "You're not useless. You just haven't done one since March." She flipped to a page titled Truing, full of small drawings. "I forget things I don't use too. The brain clears out what it thinks we don't need."
Rania looked at the notebook. "You wrote it all down?"
"Everything I only do a few times a year. And on the first Monday of each month I pick one page and actually do it on a scrap wheel, before it fades completely."
Rania smoothed the page. "So forgetting is... normal?"
"Normal. Not failing."

qa.q: What is the notebook page Beatriz shows titled?
qa.a: Truing.

qa.q: How does Beatriz seem to feel about forgetting things?
qa.a: She feels calm and unbothered, seeing forgetting as the brain clearing out what it doesn't need rather than a sign of failing.

qa.q: What habit keeps Beatriz's rarely used skills fresh?
qa.a: On the first Monday of each month she picks one notebook page and practises it on a scrap wheel.

qa.q: How might Rania feel after hearing "Normal. Not failing"?
qa.a: Rania probably feels relieved and less ashamed, and readier to lean on notes instead of self-blame.

grounding: Shows a working adult who keeps notes, reviews rarely used skills at intervals and treats forgetting as ordinary rather than failure.

passage:
Monday, first week after the monsoon break. At his new school in Nagpur, Pranav sat alone at lunch. At home he told Harish Chacha, "My old class was perfect. Everyone was my friend. We never fought."
Thursday. Harish Chacha found Pranav's old notebook while unpacking a box. Inside the back cover, in angry pencil: "Rohan and Arjun left me out AGAIN. I hate this class." Pranav read it and frowned. "I don't remember that."
Saturday. A boy from his new class, Dev, knocked with a cricket bat. Pranav hesitated at the door. "My old friends were better," he muttered. Then he looked at the notebook on the table, picked up his cap, and went out to play.

qa.q: What was written inside the back cover of Pranav's old notebook?
qa.a: "Rohan and Arjun left me out AGAIN. I hate this class."

qa.q: Why does Pranav remember his old class as perfect?
qa.a: He feels lonely at the new school, and distance has smoothed away the quarrels, so the old class feels warm and flawless.

qa.q: How could Harish Chacha help Pranav settle in?
qa.a: He could gently remind Pranav that the old class had hard days too, and encourage small chances like Dev's cricket game.

qa.q: What might Dev think if Pranav had refused to come out?
qa.a: Dev might have felt rejected and stopped knocking, never knowing Pranav was comparing him with a class that only seemed perfect.

grounding: Shows a child who moved schools remembering the old class as perfect and forgetting its quarrels.

passage:
In the coaching centre's counselling room in Kota, the ceiling fan pushed hot May air around. Joseph stared at a poster of a beach.
"I just wish I was eight again," he said. "No tests, no ranks. Just cycling and mangoes. Everything was easy."
Shalini Ma'am, the counsellor, nodded. "That sounds lovely. What else do you remember about being eight?"
He smiled. Then the smile slipped. "I was scared of the dark. I slept in Amma's room till I was ten. And I cried every morning before school because of that boy who took my tiffin."
"So not only easy."
"No." He laughed a little. "I forgot that part."
"The pressure now is real," she said. "Let's also talk about what would help this week."

qa.q: What did Joseph say he was scared of at eight?
qa.a: He was scared of the dark.

qa.q: Why does being eight feel so easy to Joseph right now?
qa.a: Under the weight of tests and ranks he feels tired and longs for comfort, so his memory keeps the cycling and mangoes and drops the fears.

qa.q: What did Shalini Ma'am do well?
qa.a: She let Joseph find the harder parts of childhood himself with one open question, without arguing, and then turned to real help for this week's pressure.

qa.q: What would change if Shalini Ma'am had just said, "Childhood wasn't easy either"?
qa.a: Joseph might have felt dismissed and defensive, and missed noticing for himself what he had forgotten.

grounding: Shows a teenager under pressure remembering early childhood as carefree and forgetting its fears.

passage:
Durga Puja drums were playing on Gargi's phone, not outside. In the small-town hostel near Dharwad, the Puja was just a date on the calendar.
She called her brother Anand. "Dada, remember our pandal-hopping? Ma's luchi, all of us on the roof? Everything was perfect at home. Here nobody even knows what Ashtami is."
Anand laughed. "Perfect? You fought with Ma every single Puja about your dress. And you hated the crowds."
"That was different," she said, curling up on the narrow bed.
On her desk lay the soil-lab report due Monday, untouched, and a note from her roommate: "Canteen at 8? Some of us are making kheer." Gargi looked at the note, then back at the old Puja photos, and kept scrolling.

qa.q: What did the roommate's note say?
qa.a: "Canteen at 8? Some of us are making kheer."

qa.q: Why does home seem perfect to Gargi right now?
qa.a: She feels homesick and lonely during Puja, and her love for home smooths out the old fights and crowds, so staying in the photos is easier than facing the report and the note.

qa.q: What small step could help Gargi this evening?
qa.a: She could go to the canteen at 8 for the kheer and open the report for a short while, and still call home.

qa.q: How does Anand see Gargi's memory of home?
qa.a: Anand remembers it more honestly and gently teases her about fighting with Ma over dresses and hating the crowds.

grounding: Shows a student far from home idealising home life while turning away from the tasks and chances in front of her.

passage:
Every Sunday lunch at Bhavna Bua's house ends the same way. She pushes back her plate and says, "In our time everything was better. People were honest, food was pure, children respected elders. We had nothing and we were happy."
My cousins roll their eyes. I used to argue: no fridge, no doctor nearby, girls taken out of school at fourteen. She told us that herself once.
Last Sunday I didn't argue. I watched her face while she talked about the neem tree in the old courtyard and her mother's hands rolling rotis, and I saw that the warmth is real, even if those years were harder than she says.
So I asked, "What did the courtyard smell like, Bua?" She talked for twenty minutes, glowing. My cousin Pooja whispered, "You're so patient, Disha." It didn't feel like patience. It felt like visiting.

qa.q: What did Disha ask Bhavna Bua last Sunday?
qa.a: "What did the courtyard smell like, Bua?"

qa.q: What changed in how Disha felt while listening to Bhavna Bua last Sunday?
qa.a: Instead of irritation and the urge to argue, Disha felt tender and warm, seeing the memory's warmth as real even if the past was harder.

qa.q: Why did asking about the courtyard work better than arguing?
qa.a: It honoured what the memory means to Bua without fighting over facts, so she glowed and the bond grew stronger.

qa.q: What is it like for Bhavna Bua when someone asks about the courtyard?
qa.a: She feels listened to and valued, and talks happily for twenty minutes instead of facing rolled eyes.

grounding: Shows a young person hearing an elder praise the old days, seeing the warm memory as real though the past was harder, and listening kindly instead of arguing.

passage:
An old radio song came on while Bidisha and Naveen were folding laundry in their Kolkata flat, and she stopped, a shirt in her hands. "This played in Baba's shop every evening. The whole lane would stop to listen. Life was so simple then."
Naveen smiled. "You miss it."
"I do." She hummed along. Then she added, more slowly, "Simple, and also hard. Baba worked fourteen hours a day. We shared one bathroom with three families. Ma worried about money every month."
She hung the shirt up. "I want to keep what that lane taught me, everyone stopping for each other. But I don't want to pretend our life now is poor just because it's busier."
Naveen turned the volume up, and they finished the laundry singing, badly.

qa.q: Where did the song play every evening in Bidisha's memory?
qa.a: In Baba's shop.

qa.q: How does Bidisha feel when the song comes on?
qa.a: She feels a warm wave of nostalgia, humming along, and then a thoughtful honesty as she remembers the hard parts too.

qa.q: What makes Bidisha's way of remembering healthy?
qa.a: She enjoys the memory and keeps the value it taught, people stopping for each other, while also naming the long hours and money worries so the present doesn't seem poor.

qa.q: How might Naveen feel watching Bidisha with the song?
qa.a: Naveen seems fond and supportive, smiling and turning the volume up so they can share the memory.

grounding: Shows a person enjoying nostalgia as comfort and a source of values while reminding herself of what was also hard.

passage:
Snow still lay on the roofs of the hill village in the week after Losar, and Hrithik trudged home with his head down. He had dropped his lunch box in the slush.
Dolma Aunty was sweeping her shop steps. "Why the long face?"
"This whole week was bad," Hrithik said. "Monday I lost the race. Tuesday I got a sum wrong. Today the lunch box. And tomorrow will be bad too, I know it."
Dolma Aunty leaned on her broom. "Didn't you win the kite contest on Wednesday? And didn't your teacher put your drawing on the board?"
Hrithik blinked. He had forgotten both. "Oh. Yes."
"Sad days hide the good ones," she said, and handed him a warm momo from the steamer.

qa.q: What did Hrithik drop in the slush?
qa.a: His lunch box.

qa.q: Why does Hrithik think the whole week was bad?
qa.a: He feels sad and upset about the lunch box, so his mind only brings up bad moments and makes tomorrow look bad too.

qa.q: How did Dolma Aunty help Hrithik see the week more fairly?
qa.a: She reminded him of good moments he had forgotten, the kite contest and the drawing on the board, and handed him a warm momo.

qa.q: What might Dolma Aunty notice that Hrithik can't?
qa.a: She can see that his upset mood is picking only the bad memories, since she remembers his good news from the week.

grounding: Shows an upset child who recalls only the bad parts of his week and expects tomorrow to be bad too.

passage:
Kashish: the group chat went quiet after I posted. nobody likes me there
Vikas: it's 11 am in the winter break, everyone's asleep
Kashish: Riya just said "ok". that means she's annoyed
Vikas: Riya says ok to everything. she said ok to me yesterday about new year plans
Kashish: I failed the chem test, messed up the recital, now this. I mess everything up
Vikas: you topped the English essay last month. remember?
Kashish: that doesn't count
Vikas: you've sounded low for a few weeks, not just today. can you tell your mum or Mrs Das tonight? I'm serious
Kashish: maybe
Vikas: not maybe. today. I'll check with you at 8
Kashish (8:05 pm): told Mum. she sat with me for ages. she's calling the school counsellor tomorrow to set up a talk

qa.q: What did Riya write that Kashish read as annoyed?
qa.a: "ok".

qa.q: Why does Kashish read the quiet chat as rejection?
qa.a: Kashish's low mood makes silence and "ok" feel like proof of being disliked and brings only failures to mind, so it all feels like fact.

qa.q: What did Vikas do that helped most?
qa.a: He offered other explanations, reminded Kashish of the English essay, and pushed for telling Mum or Mrs Das that same day, checking in at 8.

qa.q: How might Mum feel when Kashish tells her?
qa.a: Mum is probably worried but glad to be told, and shows it by sitting with Kashish for ages and arranging a talk with the school counsellor.

grounding: Shows a teenager in a low mood reading neutral messages as rejection and recalling only failures, with a friend making sure a caring adult hears about it that day.

passage:
On New Year's Eve, an hour before midnight, Suraj got the email: internship accepted. He whooped so loudly the neighbours cheered.
In the next forty minutes, riding that high, he said yes to everything. Yes, he'd run the cultural fest's stage. Yes, he'd join Rohit's hackathon team. Yes, he'd help his cousin shift flats on the 6th. Yes, he'd tutor two juniors for their tests.
"All in the first week of January?" Damini asked, looking at his calendar. "That's also when your own mid-sems start."
"It'll be fine! I'm unstoppable this week." He could only picture it going well: the stage lights, the winning demo, grateful juniors.
Damini pointed at the 6th, where four things now overlapped. "Ask me again tomorrow morning, when you're just normal happy."

qa.q: What email did Suraj get an hour before midnight?
qa.a: That his internship was accepted.

qa.q: Why does saying yes to everything feel safe to Suraj?
qa.a: He is so joyful and excited that his mind only shows him things going well, so the clashes and his own mid-sems seem small.

qa.q: What is wise about Damini's suggestion?
qa.a: Deciding again the next morning, in a calmer mood, would let Suraj see the overlap on the 6th and the risk to his exams more clearly.

qa.q: How might Rohit and the juniors be affected if Suraj overcommits?
qa.a: They might be let down if he can't show up or prepare properly, even though he meant every yes.

grounding: Shows a young adult in a great mood underestimating risks and saying yes to too much.

passage:
Last week I shared a desk with Ishita on the day her project was handed to someone else without a word. I saw her go red, open her email and start typing to our director. The subject line read "Resignation".
Then she stopped. She saved it as a draft, stood up, and said, "Yamini, I'm too angry to decide anything. I'm going for a walk." She came back twenty minutes later, still tight around the mouth, but didn't open the draft.
Two days later, on Friday morning, she read it again over tea. I watched her delete half of it. What she finally sent was a request for a meeting to understand the decision.
I can't know what went on inside her. But I've sent angry emails I still regret, and she hasn't.

qa.q: What did the subject line of Ishita's first email read?
qa.a: "Resignation".

qa.q: How was Ishita feeling when she saved the email as a draft?
qa.a: She was angry, red in the face and too angry to decide anything, and she seemed to recognise that the anger was shaping the choice.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Saving the draft and rereading it two days later over tea, because her calmer self turned a resignation into a request for a meeting.

qa.q: What might Yamini take away from watching Ishita?
qa.a: Yamini, who has sent angry emails that are still regretted, sees another way: pause, walk, and decide when calm.

grounding: Shows a person noticing her anger, postponing a major message, and returning when calm to see whether her view has changed.
